violet.x: Albertus Magnus, the thirteenth century philosopher and occultist, states that coriander, valerian, and violet are love producing herbs.

violin.x: When I play it like this, it's a fiddle; when I play it like this, it's a violin.

viper.e: From Middle French vipere, from Old French vipre, from Latin vīpera, contracted from vīvipara f (“viviparous”, adj.), from vīvus (“alive”, adj.) + parere (“to bear”…
viper.x: And aggravate my folly who committed / To ſuch a viper his moſt ſacred truſt / Of ſecreſie, my ſafety, and my life.

virago.e: Borrowed from Latin virāgō (“warlike or heroic woman”, literally “manlike”).
virago.x: Joan was all Arden, grinning there, siding with her virago mother.

virginal.e: From Middle English virginal, from Middle French virginal, from Latin virginālis. The musical instrument is probably so called from being played by young girls.

virginity.e: From Middle English virginite, from Old French virginite, from Latin virginitas. Equivalent to virgin + -ity.

virile.e: From Middle French viril, from Latin virīlis, from vir (“man”, “male human”) + -īlis (suffix forming adjectives from nouns).

virility.e: From virile + -ity, from Middle French virilité, from Latin virīlitās.
virility.x: Woolen threads were an occult means, according to the Roman poet Horace, of depriving a person of virility.

virtual.e: PIE word *wiHrós The adjective is derived from Middle English vertual, virtual [and other forms], from Old French vertüal, vertüelle (modern French virtuel), or from…
virtual.x: In fact a defeat on the battlefield, Tet was a virtual victory for the North, owing to its effect on public opinion.

virtually.e: From Middle English vertually; equivalent to virtual + -ly.
virtually.x: In this case W has a diagram with 2 vertices and one edge labelled ∞, and is therefore the infinite dihedral group. Thus W is virtually ℤ.

virtue.e: From Middle English vertu, virtue, borrowed from Anglo-Norman vertu, virtu, from Latin virtus (“manliness, bravery, worth, moral excellence”), from vir (“man”).
virtue.x: Without virtue, there is no freedom.

virtuous.e: From Middle English vertuous, borrowed from Anglo-Norman vertuous, vertous, ultimately from Late Latin virtuōsus, from Latin virtūs. By surface analysis, virtue + -ous.
virtuous.x: Successful communities need strong, selfless leaders and a virtuous people.

virulence.e: From Middle French virulence, from Late Latin virulentia.
virulence.x: This strain has higher virulence than most others.

virulent.e: PIE word *wisós From Middle English virulent (“leaking or seeping pus, purulent.
virulent.x: The politicians were virulent in their hatred of the president.

viscosity.e: From Middle French viscosité, from Old French viscosité, from Medieval Latin viscositas; analysable as viscous + -ity.

viscount.e: From Anglo-Norman viscounte, from Medieval Latin vicecomes, from Latin vice + comes. Equivalent to vice- + count. Doublet of vicecomes and vicomte.

viscous.e: First attested in 1605. Borrowed from Middle French visqueux and Late Latin viscōsus, from Latin viscum (“birdlime”). Doublet of viscose.

visibility.e: From Middle French visibilité, from Late Latin visibilitas; equivalent to visible + -ity.
visibility.x: The visibility from that angle was good.

visible.e: From Middle English visible, from Old French visible, from Late Latin visibilis (“that may be seen”), from Latin videre (“to see”), past participle visus; see vision.
visible.x: When the sun rises, the world becomes visible.

visibly.x: He was visibly upset while reading the news live on air about the school shooting.

visor.e: From Middle English viser, from Anglo-Norman viser and Old French visiere.
visor.x: No visor does become black villainy So well as soft and tender flattery.

vista.e: Borrowed from Italian vista (“view, sight”), from visto, past participle of vedere (“to see”), from Latin vidēre (“to see”). Compare vision, video, visa.
vista.x: Open up vistas of expansion into hitherto untapped markets.

visualization.x: She used visualization techniques to prepare for the competition.

visualize.e: From visual + -ize (suffix forming verbs denoting the doing or making of what is denoted by the adjectives or nouns to which it is attached).

vitality.e: From vital + -ity, from Middle French vitalité, from Latin vitalitas (“vital force, life”), from vitalis (“vital”); see vital.
vitality.x: The city’s cultural vitality impressed the visitors.

vitiligo.x: In the weeks that followed, I began to notice other people with vitiligo. On the streets, in the stores, in their cars. My God, they were everywhere!

vitriol.e: From Middle English vitriol, from Old French vitriol, from Medieval Latin vitriolum (“sulfuric acid”), from vitrum (“glass”).

vivacious.e: From Latin vīvāx (“lively, vigorous”) + -acious, from vīvere (“to live”).

vivacity.x: The one entertained me with her vivacity when I was gay, the other with her sense when I was serious.

vivisection.e: From Latin vīvus (“alive”) + sectiō (“cutting”). Compare French vivisection. See also vivid and section.

vixen.e: Alteration of earlier fixen, from Middle English fixen, fixene, from Old English *fyxen (compare also Old English fyxe (“female fox”)), from Proto-West Germanic *fuhsini…
vixen.x: The stag gets a thrill from watching his vixen have sex with another man.

vizier.e: From Ottoman Turkish وزیر (vezir) (Turkish vezir) (via French vizir), from Arabic وَزِير (wazīr, “helper, aide, minister”, literally “one who bears (the burden of…
vizier.x: Momus is not otherwise attested as Zeus’s advisor, but in name and function he matches Apsu’s vizier Mummu.

vocabulary.x: My Russian vocabulary is very limited.

vocal.x: Best cuts: "The Evil Dude," "Kung Fu, Too!" "Mama Love," "New Orleans" (with a punchy vocal by Teresa Brewer).

vocation.x: The Catholic Church supports and teaches us that there are three vocations: the single life, married life, and the religious life or priesthood.

vociferous.x: They crowded around him with vociferous welcome, Brown leading in a series of wild cheers.

vogue.x: Miniskirts were the vogue in the '60s.

voiced.x: The unvoiced signal is smaller energy than voiced signal and, so, this section is applied the smaller threshold.

voiceless.x: I've come to see she is a voiceless person in her world, and so I try to remember to stop and give her my full-faced attention when I see her.

voicing.x: Pete dressed Eddie's high-pitched voicings in the stick-sweet strings of the Philadelphia Symphony Orchestra.

voivode.e: Variously from a number of Slavic languages including Bulgarian войвода (vojvoda), Czech vojevoda, Polish wojewoda, Russian воево́да (vojevóda), and Serbo-Croatian…
voivode.x: Who was it but one of my own race who as Voivode crossed the Danube and beat the Turk on his own ground? This was a Dracula indeed!

volatile.e: From Middle French volatile, from Latin volātilis (“flying; swift; temporary; volatile”), from volō (“to fly”).
volatile.x: Now Mr. Bush plans to pour more arms into this unstable region and add fuel to the volatile powderkeg he has foolishly created.

volatility.x: The recent volatility has come with the S&P 500 hovering just above bear market territory, or a 20 percent drop from its most recent high.

volcanic.e: From French volcanique, from volcan (“volcano”); and/or directly from volcan(o) + -ic.
volcanic.x: Jo rose indignified, Vanessa following in her volcanic wake.

volcanism.e: From French volcanisme, from volcan (“volcano”); and/or directly from volcan(o) + -ism.
volcanism.x: This rejuvenation-stage or post-erosional volcanism produces lava even more alkalic than late-stage volcanism.

volcano.e: From Italian vulcano, from Vulcano (“a small volcanic island in the Tyrrhenian Sea”), from Latin Vulcānus (“Vulcan, the Roman god of fire and metalworking”).

volcanologist.x: An underwater volcano off the coast of Oregon is gearing up for an eruption, according to volcanologists who are monitoring for activity.

volition.x: Out of all the factors that can influence a person’s decision, none can match the power of his or her own volition.

volley.e: From Middle French volée (“flight”), from Vulgar Latin volta, from Late Latin volatus.
volley.x: Each volley tells that thousands cease to breathe.

voltage.e: From volt + -age, ultimately derived from the name of Alessandro Volta, inventor of the modern battery.
voltage.x: The voltage between the wires is too low to produce a spark.

volume.e: From Middle English volume, from Old French volume, from Latin volūmen (“book, roll”), from volvō (“roll, turn about”).
volume.x: The room is 9×12×8, so its volume is 864 cubic feet.

voluminous.e: From Late Latin voluminosus, from volumen, from volvō (“roll, turn about”) + -men (noun-forming suffix). Related to volume.
voluminous.x: I remember that the Baroness was clad in a voluminous silk dress, pale grey in colour, and adorned with flounces and a crinoline and train.

voluntary.e: From Middle English voluntarie, from Old French volontaire, from Latin voluntārius (“willing, of free will”), from voluntās (“will, choice, desire”), from volēns, present…
voluntary.x: She fell, to lust a voluntary prey.

voluptuous.e: From Middle French voluptueux, from Latin voluptuōsus (“delightful”), from voluptās (“pleasure, delight”), from volup (“with pleasure”).
voluptuous.x: The plentiful blankets and the voluptuous pillows of the bed called out to my tired body.

vomit.e: From Middle English vomiten, from Latin vomitāre (“vomit repeatedly”), frequentative form of vomō (“be sick, vomit”), from Proto-Indo-European *wemh₁- (“to spew, vomit”).
vomit.x: She snapped and started vomiting curses at us.

vomiting.x: Epilepsies, or fallings and reelings, and beastly vomitings. The least of these, even when the tongue begins to be untied, is a degree of drunkenness.

voracious.x: His appetite is voracious by suppertime.

voracity.e: First attested in 1526 from Middle French voracité, from Latin vorācitās (whence -acity), from vorāx.
voracity.x: Beatrice felt heart-sick to see the famished voracity with which her father ate—it was the first time he had tasted food for three days.

voter.x: The exact question being put to voters for a yes or no answer is: “Should Iceland reopen accession negotiations with the European Union?”

vowel.x: Hawaiian has either five or twenty-five vowels, depending on how they are counted.

voyage.e: From Middle English viage, borrowed from Anglo-Norman viage and Old French voiage, from Latin viaticum.

vulgar.e: From Middle English vulgare, from Latin vulgāris, from volgus, vulgus (“mob; common folk”), from Proto-Indo-European *welH-.
vulgar.x: Also the rule of false position, with dyuers examples not onely vulgar, but some appertaynyng to the rule of Algeber.

vulgarian.e: From vulgar + -ian. Compare Late Latin vulgārius, Latin vulgāris.

vulnerability.x: The country recognized their defence vulnerability after an airplane landed in front of the central square without any consequences.

vulture.e: Borrowed into Middle English from Anglo-Norman vultur, from Old French voutoir, voutre, from Latin vultur, voltur. Displaced native Old English ūf.
vulture.x: Within ten minutes of the accident, the vultures appeared and were organizing lawsuits.

vulva.e: Learned borrowing from Latin vulva, earlier volva (“womb, female sexual organ”), probably from volvō (“to turn, wrap around”).
vulva.x: The wedge-shaped character was the triangle, the archaic Paleolithic sign of the vulva; the pubic triangle was at the end of the phallic stylus.

vuvuzela.e: Borrowed from Zulu vuvuzela (“to make a vu vu noise”), from the /vuː/ sound the horns make.
vuvuzela.x: When the Manchester United squad walked through the arrival gates at Durban International yesterday, most players heard a vuvuzela for the first time.
